stories.headline: 'Kings of Manchester': City boss Enzo Maresca defends Elliot Anderson's claim ahead of derby
stories.summary: Enzo Maresca believes Elliot Anderson was justified in describing Manchester City as the "kings of Manchester."
stories.body:
Enzo Maresca believes Elliot Anderson was justified in describing Manchester City as the "kings of Manchester."

The England midfielder made the claim after completing his £116 million ($156m) move to City from Nottingham Forest in the summer.

The 23-year-old's comments could mean he gets a hostile reception in his first Manchester derby on Sunday as City face arch rivals United at Old Trafford in the Premier League.

Maresca recognises that, historically, United have been the bigger club but, given recent successes, he can see why those of a younger generation such as Anderson might regard City as the dominant force.

The City manager said: "Probably the reason why Elliot said that is because he grew up in the last 15 years. I think Manchester City were unbelievable in what they achieved.

"So it was normal when Elliot said that. If you go back it's a different picture, but for me the reason Elliot said that is because when he grew up Manchester City was dominant."

City are boosted by the return of England left-back Nico O'Reilly after a back issue.

O'Reilly has missed the last two games after pulling up in the warm-up prior to last weekend's victory over Coventry.

"Nico is 100% available," said Maresca, who added that winger Jérémy Doku remains on the sidelines with a calf problem.

It is Maresca's first derby since succeeding Pep Guardiola as manager but he has previous experience of the fixture having worked on the City backroom staff. He has also been involved in numerous other derbies throughout his career and it is an encounter he is relishing.

- O'Reilly set to return for Man City in derby

- Weekend predictions: Who wins Manchester derby?

- Is Erling Haaland the Premier League's only global superstar?

The Italian said: "We know how important a derby is, especially here, for the club, for the fans, for everyone.

"It is a special game and the most important thing we can do is to try to be ourselves, in the way we have been until today. Then we will see the final result.

"I have been involved in different ones. I promise you the worst is Olympiakos-Panathinaikos. I have been in Italy with Juventus-Torino, Sevilla-Betis, as a manager with Chelsea -- different ones.

"I know Old Trafford is quite different but the main focus for the players has to be the game plan, how we can win, how we can press, how we can be better. I want these kind of games, I like them."

City go into the game after winning their opening three Premier League matches, while United's start has been mixed, with Michael Carrick's side having collected four points so far.

City have had an extra two days of rest following their Champions League game at Porto on Tuesday, as United were in action against Sabah on Thursday, but Maresca does not think that will be significant.

"Sometimes it happens in football," he said. "I don't have any doubt that Man United are going to be ready.

"It just matters to adapt. It happened last year with us, this season with them. Next season it will happen with a different team."

stories.headline: NBA intel: What to expect at next week's owners' meetings
stories.summary: The next steps in the Clippers investigation, league expansion and NBA Europe could all be decided next week.
stories.body:
Adam Silver, now in his 12th year as NBA commissioner, has dealt with plenty of changes and challenges during his tenure. But Monday and Tuesday's board of governors meeting in New York represents an inflection point for the league. And his leadership will play a major role.

There are a few main agenda items that could set major events into motion that, in some cases, have been years in the making.

Most of the work by Silver and the league office has been done in the months leading up to this meeting, where the presentations and formal votes might happen, but the public rollout is a big responsibility for the commissioner, who will deliver his news conference Tuesday.

This BOG meeting has the potential to be one of more consequential ones in recent memory. Here are three topics I'm expecting Silver and the owners to discuss: the LA Clippers' investigation and punishments, NBA Europe and the next steps in expansion.

Official statements on the Clippers' salary cap circumvention punishment
Silver spoke loudly with his actions last week, slapping the Clippers with five revoked first-round draft picks and a record $30 million fine. But how he responds in front of cameras for the first time next week will set the tone going forward as this situation probably has another chapter or two to come.
The Clippers have not publicly accepted their fate or announced whether they will pursue legal action. They have not said who will act as the governor at the meeting in suspended owner Steve Ballmer's place or who will act as interim head of basketball operations in place of the suspended Lawrence Frank.

They also have not executed the trade to send Kawhi Leonard to the Toronto Raptors, a deal agreed to on the first day of free agency.

This purposeful inaction, in addition to the legal saber-rattling, can be seen as the Clippers leaving open their options and negotiation windows.

When the NBA issued its enormous penalty -- the final revoked draft pick in 2034 -- it did so knowing Ballmer might have a litigious reaction. Whether it would admit it, the league has also given itself room to negotiate. (The league and the Clippers reportedly had failed settlement discussions before the Wachtell, Lipton report was made public. )

One topic rival front offices have discussed is the less-talked-about but draconian-sounding "compliance and monitoring program by the league office for a period of five years" penalty that was also leveled on the Clippers. The terms were nebulous, probably for a reason, and the devil will surely be in the details.

"Are they going to be reading all their emails, reading their texts, listening to their phone calls?" one general manager told ESPN. "I have no idea what that [penalty] means."

The announcement of the penalty and the side deal the league cut with the players' union to have Leonard accept a $700,000 reimbursement penalty and eliminate the Clippers' option to take the NBA to arbitration, certainly changed the dynamic.

During the investigation, which spanned five major Silver news conferences, he repeatedly gave no indication of the severity of the findings, even though he said he was getting regular updates.

In the past two, before Game 1 of the 2026 Finals and after the July owners meeting in Las Vegas, Silver gave off some Judge Judy meme vibes by figuratively tapping his watch and saying the investigation needed to wrap up. It was not the posture of someone about to release a bombshell. And the Clippers, based on their public and private statements claiming shock, certainly didn't see it coming.

David Stern, Silver's legendary predecessor, was known for fiery news conferences when announcing major disciplinary actions, whether it was after the 2004 Malice at the Palace in Detroit or when he levied his own five-pick penalty to the Minnesota Timberwolves for salary cap violations in 2000. Silver is typically much more measured and disarming. When he suspended former Phoenix Suns owner Robert Sarver three years ago, Silver was even-tempered.

Soon after the report was released and the punishments announced, the Clippers issued an emotional statement and sent a seething letter to Silver. Here comes the next round.

The latest on NBA Europe -- with a possible international showdown looming
For much of the past two years, the league has been planning a major push into Europe. And recent reports have set the stage for a drama.

The Euroleague, which would be NBA Europe's main rival, is waiting for a formal offer of a partnership in the very near future and has scheduled a rare owners meeting for Oct. 5 near Lake Como in northern Italy, where it all could come to a head.

The NBA has gone through several rounds of bids and is ready to move forward with a 16-team league with 12 permanent members and four rotating members, starting in 2027. League officials have said there are bidding groups for 12 of those new teams in Europe, with franchises in London and Paris expected to go for $1 billion-plus, per league sources.

But the NBA's preference would be to blend existing Euroleague teams and new franchises into one pan-European league with NBA branding and leadership, Euroleague history and infrastructure, plus the international organization of FIBA.

That sounds nice, of course, but there's so much money and power at stake that the process to do so will be bumpy, at best.

Top officials from both the NBA and the Euroleague have said they are prepared to work together or go it alone in what surely would be an unsustainable fragmented system. It could be a seminal showdown and will be a major part of this owners meeting, multiple sources said.

The next step in NBA (domestic) expansion
The meeting could feature a vote -- or perhaps the scheduling of a vote -- to move forward with expansion, which has been long assumed but never formalized. Silver, who has said the league has been working with bankers on vetting ownership groups, could establish an exact timetable for choosing winning bids or announcing finalists.
It should not be assumed that both Las Vegas and Seattle will be on the same schedule or be close to the same price point, ownership sources said. Preliminary bidders in the $8 billion range for Vegas quickly learned the number would be higher, sources said. A Seattle team, meanwhile, could be sold for considerably less.

Some teams have been projecting the per-team payout for expansion to be $500 million to $600 million, which would put the combined expansion fee at around $15 billion to $18 billion.

Within a few months, the Los Angeles Lakers sale could close for $12.5 billion; expansion could generate a once-in-a-generation windfall for teams while also increasing their valuations; and NBA Europe might generate billions more.

With the future of those nine-, 10- and 11-figure sums potentially at stake, it's difficult to understate the importance of next week's BOG meeting for Silver and the NBA.

stories.headline: Spanish Grand Prix in Madrid LIVE: F1 practice updates, results and analysis
stories.summary: The first practice session at the Spanish Grand Prix is due to get under way as drivers will get a feel for the Madring for the first time.
stories.body:
Mercedes' George Russell topped the times in the first practice session at the Spanish Grand Prix, and you can follow live updates here on ESPN.

Drivers across the grid have predicted that the brand-new circuit is the "most risky" on the Formula 1 calendar.

Practice two will begin at 4 p.m. BST.

- Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc held face-to-face talks after Monza woes: 'It's healthy'

- Spanish Grand Prix: Everything you need to know about F1's brand-new Madring

- Spanish Grand Prix 2026: Race start time in Madrid, how to watch, full schedule, predictions

The Madring is a hybrid between a street circuit and a purpose-built track, using a mixture of public roads and private land around the IFEMA Madrid exhibition centre.

The circuit is 5.416km long and features 22 corners. Sunday's race will take place over 57 laps.

Formula 1 is returning to Madrid for the first time since 1981, when the Spanish Grand Prix was held at Jarama, around 30 kilometres north of the city.

Mercedes' George Russell said ahead of the weekend: "I would put it, arguably, as the most risky circuit of the whole calendar, because you have real high-speed corners, sort of Jeddah-esque. The walls are very close. There's no margin for error.

"But then, you have other corners that are quite like Baku, where you're coming from a high speed into a slow braking zone. You're braking and turning at the same time.

"So, locking tyres is going to be easy. If you're not coping, you'll be straight in the wall.

"I think it's going to be really challenging for us as drivers. The race is going to be challenging to overtake. So, on the whole, it's not an easy one."

Alpine's Pierre Gasly added: "I must say it's exciting, but at the same time I think it's going to be quite a disruptive weekend, how easy it will be to have a crash."

stories.headline: Kings' Kevin Fiala has further surgery, to miss start of camp
stories.summary: Kings forward Kevin Fiala will miss the start of training camp after undergoing follow-up surgery for the broken leg he sustained during the Milan Cortina Olympics.
stories.body:
LOS ANGELES -- Kings forward Kevin Fiala will miss the start of training camp after undergoing follow-up surgery for the broken leg he sustained during the Milan Cortina Olympics.

Fiala missed the second half of the NHL season and the playoffs after he was hurt playing for Switzerland in a preliminary round game on Feb. 13. He broke his left femur in a collision with Canada forward Tom Wilson and had to be stretchered off the ice. He had surgery in Italy.

Fiala had 18 goals and 22 assists in 56 games for the Kings last season. The 30-year-old winger has been one of Los Angeles' top offensive contributors since being acquired in a trade from the Minnesota Wild in June 2022 as a restricted free agent. The Kings then signed him to a seven-year contract.

The Kings did not announce a timeline for Fiala's recovery. Los Angeles plays its season opener at the Colorado Avalanche on Sept. 30, a rematch of the four-game sweep that marked the Kings' fifth straight first-round exit.

stories.headline: Team USA scores 108 in rout of Hungary to reach FIBA semis
stories.summary: The U.S. routed Hungary 108-56 to advance to the semifinals of the women's FIBA World Cup and stretched its winning streak in the tournament to 34 games.
stories.body:
BERLIN -- After a scare in the group phase against Italy, Team USA knew it wouldn't be able to play poorly in the knockout rounds of the FIBA World Cup if it wanted to come away with a fifth straight gold medal and 12th overall.

It was only the quarterfinals, but the U.S. responded to that challenge, putting together what the team viewed as its best performance of the tournament with a 108-56 drilling of Hungary. The Americans' 108 points and 31 assists were both records for a World Cup quarterfinal game.

Napheesa Collier led all scorers with 19 points -- a personal best with the senior national team -- followed by 15 from Rhyne Howard and 10 each from Kahleah Copper, Caitlin Clark and Jackie Young.

"We talked about just getting better with each game, and I think we did that today, especially with how we shared [the ball]," Howard said. "I think if we continue to play like that and continue to keep everybody on the same page, continue to move the ball, it's going to be really hard to stop us."

Added Collier: "We were moving the ball a lot. It wasn't one-on-one. We were looking for a great shot, not just a good shot, and so when we play that way, it's really fun. And I feel like our chemistry is building each game."

The U.S. will face either Spain or Australia in Saturday's semifinal, which will tip at 2 p.m. ET.

The Americans got out to a hot start, jumping ahead 36-12 at the end of the first quarter and leading 59-30 at the half. Their defense frustrated Hungary, which saw star post duo Dorka Juhasz and Virag Takacs-Kiss combine for just four points.

The U.S. had 25 of its 44 points off turnovers at the half, using defense to fuel offense on the other end.

"Everybody's just all dialed in offensively and defensively," said Angel Reese, who finished with nine points, six rebounds and three assists. "We talked about our keys, what it's going to take to win gold, and I think tonight we did everything that coach asked us to do."

Two games after Italy held the U.S. to 55 points, the Americans got mostly whatever they wanted offensively. Their 58.8% field goal percentage was their best clip of the tournament, and 12 3-pointers matched their tournament high after shooting 29% from deep in the group stage.

Team USA also won the inside battle Thursday, its 32 paint points at the half (52 overall) were more than the entire Hungary team had scored at that point.

"I feel like today was a really good one for us," Collier said. "We worked on some defensive schemes that we wanted to get better at, some offensive stuff that we wanted to clean up, and so I feel like we went out and executed that."

The 108 points marked the second most scored in a knockout game in World Cup history, behind only Brazil's 110 against the U.S. in the 1994 semifinals. The 52-point win margin was the second largest for a quarterfinal in World Cup history.

"I thought it started with our activity on the defensive end," coach Kara Lawson said. "And so our ability to turn them over, get out in transition, get some advantage plays, 2-on-1, 3-on-2, I thought gave us a lot of confidence early. And then our ability to shoot the 3-point shot ... we have a really good 3-point shooting team, and so I just thought that's what kind of jump-started us."

Lawson and the players agreed the performance was a product of their expedited chemistry-building finally starting to come into fruition. Unlike many national teams, the U.S. did not have a training camp or much prep time together before arriving in Berlin, last gathering as a group (and not its final roster) at the Final Four in April. They have now been together for about 10 days after leaving their WNBA teams.

"The more we play, the more comfortable we're getting with each other," said Young, the only American to hit double figures in each game this tournament. "And tonight we got the ball popping and we were able to get some easy buckets in transition."

Added Collier: "Today felt good, not just because of the score, but in the way that we were scoring as well."

stories.headline: Broncos hand down review, with 'new Te'o' confirmed
stories.summary: Brisbane have revealed the findings of their season review after finishing a diabolical 14th, but sackings of coaching staff are not on the agenda.
stories.body:
Brisbane have handed down their review findings after a shocking NRL season, which will result in an additional assistant coach being recruited and Matt Ballin officially taking charge of defence.

Head coach Michael Maguire will stay on and complete the third year of his tenure after he led the Broncos to a premiership in 2025, then 14th place this year.

The stunning fall from grace was due to a variety of factors, but key was the defensive collapse, where the Broncos conceded 677 points, their worst since 2021 when they let in 695 points.

The 2020 wooden-spoon season, just 20 games due to COVID, remains the lowest in points per match conceded with 31.2, but this year's 28.2 was also unacceptable.

The Broncos lacked a regular defensive coach after Ben Te'o resigned early in the season after disagreements with Maguire.

Manly's 2011 premiership winner and Queensland assistant coach Ballin, already on staff as an assistant and highly respected for his talents overall in the coaching space, will take charge of making sure Brisbane's defensive structures are secure.

Broncos CEO Dave Donaghy informed club members on Friday of the review results in a lengthy letter.

"We will invest further in our coaching and development resources, supporting our head coach Michael Maguire, who last year became only the second coach in our club's history to win a premiership," Donaghy said.

"Trent Barrett will continue as attack coach and Matt Ballin will assume responsibility for defence.

"Adam Brideson remains as a development coach and will be supported by another coach in this space, such is its importance to preparing our players for the rigours of the NRL."

In his letter Donaghy said the club reviewed good years and bad.

"When it became clear that we wouldn't play finals this season, we commenced a detailed review of our football program - to understand what worked, what didn't and the controllable and uncontrollable factors that impacted our season," he said.

Donaghy outlined "five priority areas" to ensure the club would "bounce back strongly in 2027".

Football leadership was one area, with current general manager of the NRL program Troy Thomson becoming executive general manager of football.

Donaghy said that would provide "greater alignment across our NRL, pathway and development programs".

The beefed-up coaching resources will be complemented by an upgraded investment in the academy program.

"With expansion to 20 clubs and continued growing competition in our own backyard, we want to ensure our staff are equipped to take the fight up head on," Donaghy said.

The club's pre-season preparation will be realigned, with less long-distance travel. That was necessary last year with the Broncos playing in the World Club Challenge, but a lengthy pre-season training camp in Toowoomba was also not received well by several players and staff.

"Our priority for the 2027 pre-season, though, will be to limit travel to within Australia and New Zealand," Donaghy said.

"The objective is to give our players and coaches the best possible preparation for next year's season-opener."

The final area Donaghy addressed was the woeful record at Suncorp Stadium, where the Broncos lost 12 of 14 games.

"An obvious area we need to improve," he said.

stories.headline: Andoni Iraola calls for Liverpool to start quicker in games: 'Everything looks easier'
stories.summary: Andoni Iraola wants to see his Liverpool side make a fast start in Saturday's Premier League clash with Fulham to avoid another match where they need to come from behind.
stories.body:
Andoni Iraola wants to see his Liverpool side make a fast start in Saturday's Premier League clash with Fulham to avoid another match where they need to come from behind.

Iraola has made an unbeaten start to life at Anfield, but Liverpool have conceded first in three of his opening four games in charge, coming back to draw with Newcastle and Nottingham Forest before beating Ipswich 2-0 and coming from behind in a 2-1 win over Atlético Madrid.

Before Alexander Isak's brace sank Ipswich within the opening 10 minutes last Friday, Liverpool failed to score in the first half of their first two league games, and that is something Iraola is keen to change.

"I think the team has goals in it," Iraola said. "In all the games we've been dangerous, we've created chances, we scored two goals [in every game], we could have scored more in some of those games, but now it's about being more efficient.

"Not conceding the two goals against Newcastle, not conceding the goals against Forest, and also when the goals come because I think we are not starting too well in the games. We had the positive precedent of Ipswich and the games look much more comfortable when you start like this.

"The other games, we started losing and then you have to do a lot of effort to come back. I would like obviously to score the first goal and then everything looks easier, but we need to have the right mentality.

"Against Atlético I think we had a chance after something like 15 seconds, Alex [Mac Allister] had a very clear chance to score and then everyone says 'incredible start,' you score and it changes, but I think the start of the games is probably one of the parts where we can be a little bit better.

"In the second half we've normally been better, but I want to try and impose ourselves from the beginning because it becomes easier, everything."

Liverpool will face a Fulham side yet to pick up a point under former Real Madrid head coach Alvaro Arbeloa, who has already come under pressure given their slow start.

"We have played just three Premier League games and to make big conclusions about any team, I think it's too early, and I think Fulham is a great example," Iraola said.

"I think they have played well in the three games, honestly. They've lost the three games by one goal. I think if you see a lot of the stats they have and you don't know the points they have, you will think they have five points at least because they've been controlling the games."

It will be a different sort of rivalry with Arbeloa for Iraola when they face each other on the touchline.

The pair were once Spain teammates, although Iraola admitted the Fulham boss usually got the better of the former Liverpool defender back then.

"I think we played maybe very few times together in the national team," Iraola said. "We were fighting more or less for the same position, but I think he was more successful in that he played more games than me!"

stories.headline: Six NFL records that could be broken during the 2026 season
stories.summary: Can a team break the NFL's rushing record? Will we see a new long in field goal kicking? Could there be a new single-season tight end receiving yardage mark?
stories.body:
The 2026 NFL season is already here. Unfortunately, through two games, no NFL record has been broken. Boring!

Last time we saw regular-season football, Myles Garrett was setting a single-season sack record (23) and Trey McBride was catching more passes (126) than any tight end in NFL history. With a 17-game season and rules skewed to favor offenses, it feels like more and more records are within reach every year.

I wanted to find more NFL records that could be broken in 2026, so I went through a long list of candidates. Among them were:

Highest average punt distance for a single season (the Cardinals' Blake Gillikin and Packers' Daniel Whelan both hit 51.7 yards per punt last season, tied for third all time).
Most receiving touchdowns in a game (Jerry Rice had five -- if it were four, I would have included it).
Most penalized team in NFL history (somehow the 17-game season isn't really affecting total penalty numbers).

After I ruled those out, I landed on a final six that could reasonably fall this season. There's some statistical reasoning for a few, some schematic considerations considered and some straight vibes rolled in. I want to see a 70-yard field goal. I want to root for a 70-yard field goal. Give me a 70-yard field goal!

But let's start with a new receiving record for tight ends.

Jump to a record:

Most TE receiving yards in a season

Most fourth-down conversions in a game

Most team rushing yards in a season

Longest field goal in NFL history

Highest completion percentage in a season

Most fumbles forced by a player in a season

Single-season receiving yards by a tight end
Current record holder: Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce (1,416 in 2020)

We have entered a new era of high-volume receiving from tight ends.

Last season, McBride was the Cardinals' only bright spot when he set a new single-season NFL record for tight end receptions with 126. He broke Zach Ertz's record of 116 receptions, which Ertz accomplished in a 16-game season (7.25 receptions per game) as a member of the Eagles in 2018. McBride's 126 in a 17-game season was even enough to beat Ertz out on a per-game basis (7.41).

Tight ends have cracked 100 receptions 13 times, and eight of them have come in the past six years. In 2024, the Raiders' Brock Bowers broke the record for all rookie receptions (not just tight ends) with his 112-catch season. As tight ends become better receivers and coordinators become more clever in featuring them, the inherent reliability of a tight end target lends itself to high reception totals. Just last season, TE targets had a 72% completion rate, while WR targets had a 62% completion rate.

So why bet on the tight end receiving yardage total to be broken? While it is generally the case that tight ends are targeted closer to the line of scrimmage and can't create explosives downfield ... there are a few exceptions to the rule.

Bears tight end Colston Loveland averaged 12.3 yards per reception over the course of the 2025 season in Ben Johnson's explosive-oriented offense -- that was third among all high-volume tight ends, and it doesn't even include his wild-card round explosion (eight catches, 137 yards) against the Packers. Because Loveland started the season slowly as a rookie coming off injury, he wasn't heavily targeted, accounting for 15.0% of the Bears' team targets relative to McBride's 27.4% with the Cardinals.

I thought Bowers would be a second excellent candidate to set the arc here, but a late meniscus surgery has him out for at least the next couple of weeks. The good news is that Bowers is far from the only young, exciting tight end looking for a spike in receiving.

Colts tight end Tyler Warren was on pace for over 1,000 yards last season before Daniel Jones fractured his fibula ahead of Week 12 and the offense suffered. With target sponge Michael Pittman Jr. off the Colts roster, Warren could more than pick up where he left off. Jaguars tight end Brenton Strange has always had the explosiveness (12.3 yards per reception) but never the volume (10.9% of the team's target share) -- but the Jaguars want more multi-TE sets this year, which should open him up as he takes on fewer blocking assignments. Lions tight end Sam LaPorta now has offensive coordinator Drew Petzing, who was McBride's playcaller when he broke out as a high-volume pass catcher over the past two seasons. And the Cardinals have a new coaching staff as well -- maybe they'll think about McBride's role a little more vertically.

I'm certain we'll see some candidates challenge the receptions record -- it's just too good of a time to be a pass-catching tight end in the NFL. But ... Kelce's 1,416 yards is a bit trickier to reach. Set in 2020 in the throes of Chiefs hype, Kelce benefitted from the ceiling-lifting speed of Tyreek Hill and the pass-happiness of head coach Andy Reid (and some of the greatest quarterback play in the history of the universe from Patrick Mahomes, of course). Even with an additional game, McBride was almost 200 yards off Kelce's total in 2025 -- he had more targets but he couldn't match Kelce for explosiveness.

Every candidate we've discussed above has a weakness in his profile.

Loveland should have explosiveness and volume within the Bears' passing game ... but Chicago runs it way more than those 2020 Chiefs did (they had the fifth-highest pass rate over expectation in the past 10 seasons, per NFL Next Gen Stats). LaPorta has the ceiling-lifting speedsters in receiver Jameson Williams and the right scheme for big explosives ... but will he get enough targets sharing time with Williams, receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown and running back Jahmyr Gibbs? Bowers should have the scheme, the volume and the big plays ... but will his quarterbacking quality be enough?

If it were easy to break a record, it would happen every year. Of all the receiving records (yards, receptions and touchdowns) across all the positions (running back, receivers and tight ends) I know I want to be betting on tight end records to fall. Bowers broke one in 2024. McBride broke one in 2025. Kelce's total yardage may be the toughest nut to crack at the position, but this new wave of big-play tight ends has the constitution for it.

Single-game fourth-down conversions
Current record holder: Los Angeles Chargers (six, 2021) and Dallas Cowboys (six, 2025)

That's right: Two teams in NFL history have successfully converted on six fourth-down tries in a single game, and one was last season.

You're forgiven for forgetting the finer details of the Cowboys' 30-23 Christmas Day win over the 4-11 Commanders, who were starting backup quarterback Josh Johnson. You were drowsy on eggnog anyway. But Dallas attempted and converted six fourth downs on the day, tying the 2021 Chargers (coached by Brandon Staley, the straw man of much fourth-down debate over the past several seasons) for the most in NFL history.

Most of the Cowboys' fourth-down attempts were unspectacular. There was a fourth-and-1 from their own 44-yard-line on the first drive. On their second drive, another fourth-and-1 -- this one at midfield -- was quickly joined by a fourth-and-2 from the Commanders' 23 and a fourth-and-1 from the Commanders' 10. According to ESPN Research, that sequence is just the third drive in the past 45 years to start in the first quarter and have three fourth-down conversions. Two of the three were last season. We live in a different world.

The Cowboys had another no-man's land conversion (fourth-and-2 from their own 45) late in the fourth quarter, then ended the game on a fourth-and-1 sneak to snag their sixth conversion.

It took a unique day of near-conversions on third downs for the Cowboys, who never had to attempt a fourth down longer than 2 yards out. These auto-go situations on fourth-and-1s are why the single-game record is easily within reach. Even as teams attempt more fourth downs than ever before (3.3 per game in 2025), their conversion rate is still rising, because the fourth downs they're attempting have a high probability of being converted. Put another way: Average distance to the first on fourth downs is decreasing.

As more teams go for it on fourth-and-1s -- and call plays on third down with those auto-gos in mind -- the potential for a huge spike week increases. Last season featured both the most games with five or more fourth-down conversions (three) and the most with four or more fourth-down conversions (seven) in NFL history. (A 17-game schedule sure helps.) There were also 47 games with three or more fourth-down conversions in 2025, beating the previous record (set in 2024) ... of 34.

The tricky thing about seven fourth-down conversions is that it requires seven fourth-down attempts, which is hard to reach. In order to get to fourth down, an offense has to get beyond first, second and third down -- all without losing so much yardage that going for the fourth is untenable. The average NFL offense had 26.8 first-down plays per game last season -- the lowest single-season number this century, as pace of play has declined and defenses are resurgent. To break the record, seven of those 27 potential series need to become a fourth down (26%), and then all seven need to be converted. That's not easy!

We've also seen a big spike in fourth-down aggressiveness. A whopping 23.4% of fourth downs were attempted last season -- a huge leap from the 20.0% from 2024. Field position is a big part of that jump, as drives that start closer to the 50 get to the 50 more often, which is the area of the field in which fourth downs are most often attempted. The field position factor feels like it's here to stay, but we can't know that for sure. The total number of fourth-down tries could still decline in 2026.

Still, I'm willing to bet that we see seven fourth-down conversions in a game sooner rather than later. If not this year, then in a season soon to come.

Single-season rushing yards
Current record holder: Baltimore Ravens (3,189 in 2024)

In the research process for this piece, I learned that the 1948 San Francisco 49ers (sick logo, by the way) rushed for 3,663 yards. In fourteen games, no less! Johnny Strzykalski led the team with 906 rushing yards from his right halfback position. Seven players had at least 250 rushing yards, including Verl Lillywhite and Len Eshmont (incredible, real names). What a time to be alive.

Anyway, this was long before the Super Bowl era began in 1967. With reverence, let's place the '48 Niners atop a dusty shelf and focus instead on the 3,189 rushing yards produced by the 2024 Ravens. It was their first season with running back Derrick Henry aligned beside quarterback Lamar Jackson, and man, it went great. Henry had 1,921 yards while Jackson added 915 -- his highest mark of the past five seasons, thanks in part to being healthy for all 17 games.

It was a resurgent season for rushing overall, as offenses swung hard against the two-high shell revolution. Running back carries that season produced 4.4 yards per attempt (tied for the highest mark in a season this century) and 2.47 yards before contact per attempt (highest for a season since 2020). Throw in the best QB rushing season of recent memory -- 20.3 yards per game and 4.7 yards per rush, both highs for this century -- and you have the right environment for a record-setting year.

The Ravens' gross rushing production diminished in 2025 in much the same way the rest of the league's did. While running back carries stayed up, quarterback runs became less explosive as Jackson, the Commanders Jayden Daniels and the Eagles' Jalen Hurts dealt with injuries and reduced riskiness on the run. If we're going to get a season the likes of that 2024 Ravens year, we need a team willing to run their quarterback again at a high volume ... and an elite handoff game to boot.

The 2026 Ravens are clearly the best candidate to pull this off. They replaced both starting guards (John Simpson and rookie Olaivavega Ioane in for Daniel Faalele and Andrew Vorhees), which should improve their downhill rushing attack even with center Tyler Linderbaum gone in free agency. Jackson also spoke openly about his injury struggles in 2025 and his belief he can return to pre-injury form -- that could mean another season of 800 or 900 rushing yards.

A big part of high rushing totals is plenty of garbage time, and the Ravens were middle of the pack in offensive plays with a pre-snap win probability of 90% or higher last season (159 total). As a testament to the unique effect of Henry, who seemingly gets better as games go on, the Ravens had 5.1 yards per rush on their 100 garbage-time carries, second only to the Colts.

The only other team that runs its quarterback enough to potentially challenge this number is the Bills, who led 2025 with 2,714 rushing yards and were third in QB-specific rushing at 585. They retained their offensive coordinator in Joe Brady, now the head coach, and the current theory is that he'll crank up the pass now that he's at the helm but maybe still let Josh Allen run a little more in the process.

The Commanders are one more team to watch here, as they were third in rushing yards in 2024 thanks in part to the dual-threat revelation of Daniels. He missed time with injuries in 2025, and new offensive coordinator David Blough is running more of an under-center offense that will limit his designed runs. But I'm optimistic this could create a healthier rushing attack overall.

Also important to watch is Washington's total plays compared to the rest of the league. Partially because of a heavy dose of no-huddle, the Commanders were the second-fastest offense in terms of seconds elapsed per play in 2024. That number dropped in 2025, but it could leap again with Daniels back under center.

It feels a little boring to predict the 2026 Ravens to beat a record set by the 2024 Ravens. But the larger league trends lean toward the running game getting easier and easier as defenses play lighter personnel, even against multi-TE sets. Healthy offenses will continue zagging where defenses zig, so rushing attempts and totals should climb in 2026.

Longest field goal
Current record holder: Jaguars kicker Cam Little (68 yards, 2025)

This might be a super boring one, as it was just set last year by the big-legged Little in Week 9 against the Raiders. (It wasn't even his biggest kick of the year! His 70-yard preseason masterstroke, regrettably, does not qualify for the history books.) But I like big kicks and I want to talk about them.

The average field goal attempted was 40.5 yards last season, marking 2025 and 2024 as the only seasons this century with an average over 40 yards. That number is deepening for two reasons. The first is we're going for fewer short field goals, as teams have elected for more fourth-down tries in the red zone. The league attempted 210 field goals of under 30 yards in 2025, the fewest such attempts this century.

But that's not what we care about when it comes to a kicking record. We care about the fact that as the 20-yard field goals have disappeared, the 60-yarders have replaced them. The league attempted 22 field goals of 60-plus yards last season, which is as many as teams attempted from 2000 to 2008 combined.

The 2025 leap in 60-plus-yard field goals can be partially explained by the rule change to "K-balls." Whereas teams previously had only a few pregame hours to doctor their K-balls to the preferred feel of their specialists, they can now work on them all season long. This allows kickers to practice with the same balls they'll use on gameday, and in turn, kick them more effectively. Whether or not the K-ball alone is increasing field goal distance, or if it's in conjunction with better technique and easier playing surfaces, is debated within the league. But there's no doubt that longer field goals are more attainable.

Still ... a 70-yarder? Only four have been attempted in the regular season this century, and only eight have come in the Super Bowl era. The most recent was a 2024 70-yarder from the Cowboys' Brandon Aubrey that was tipped at the line. Unsurprisingly, this kick came with the clock expiring at the end of the first half (when the field position given to the opposing team after a missed kick wouldn't matter). The longest field goal attempted this century with more than a minute left in the half was another Aubrey try -- only 65 yards.

So for this record to fall in 2026, we need to get lucky with a huge-legged kicker on an end-of-half opportunity. Little and Aubrey are the only two kickers to have made multiple 65-plus-yard kicks; Buccaneers kicker Chase McLaughlin has hit his lone try. Jake Bates has been given two chances of 65-plus by the Lions and is 0-for-2, but he had the length on a 67-yarder.

Maybe 70 yards will prove a hard limit even as more 60-somethings are attempted. To kick a 69-yard field goal, after all, is to have the line of scrimmage at your own 48-yard line. But my guess is that we'll see at least one 70-yard attempt this season. And so long as we get the attempt, we might well get the make.

Single-season completion percentage by a quarterback
Current record holder: retired quarterback Drew Brees (74.4% in 2018)

This is an interesting one. As an early point of clarity, there are many quarterbacks who ended their seasons with a completion percentage of 100% -- mostly on one or two attempts. The threshold Pro Football Reference uses for completion percentage is that a quarterback attempts at least 14 passes per team game -- 224 in a 16-game season, and 238 in a 17-game season.

Under this condition, it's 2018 Brees at the top and 2019 Brees (74.3%) right behind -- his age-39 and age-40 seasons. But players have knocked on the door. Tua Tagovailoa and Jared Goff (both 2024) are third and fourth on this list at 72.9% and 72.4%, respectively. Drake Maye hit 72.0% in 2025, tied with 2017 Brees for fifth. This one's coming down soon.

The 70% threshold has only recently been breached with regularity. Before 2000, only three quarterbacks did it (minimum 200 pass attempts): Ken Anderson in 1982, Joe Montana in 1989 and Steve Young in 1994. The next six times came over 2009 to 2017 -- and four of those were Brees. But then Kirk Cousins did it in 2018 (alongside Brees). Both Derek Carr and Ryan Tannehill did it in 2019 (again alongside Brees). Aaron Rodgers and Deshaun Watson did it in 2020 (of course, alongside Brees).

It doesn't take spectacular talent to clear 70%. Joe Burrow did it in 2021 with the Bengals, but then Jake Browning also did it two years later. The particular play style of the Zac Taylor Bengals -- a lot of shotgun, two elite receivers, quick throws from spread formations -- lends itself to high completion percentages. And Browning was playing the way a backup should, taking the high percentage throws. When five quarterbacks did it in 2024, the elite (Burrow), the good (Goff, Baker Mayfield) and the average (Geno Smith, Tagovailoa) were all represented.

Betting on a quarterback to beat Brees' mark of 74.4% isn't so much a bet on quarterbacks as it is a general bet on offensive health. The league's best offenses are better than the league's best offenses have ever been. When everything clicks, a 70% completion rate is far more easily reachable.

This is doubly true as quarterbacks continue to scramble more often (they're currently doing it at historic rates). Scrambles remove bad pass attempts, like late heaves or pressured checkdowns or throwaways. By cutting the chaff of the worst pass attempts, we raise the completion percentage overall.

The Chargers feel like the best bet for that particular constellation of elite quarterback, pass catcher and play designer. Justin Herbert has been eerily consistent in his completion rates, as five of his six pro seasons have ended with a completion rate between 65% and 67%. But he has never enjoyed a playcaller who creates as many high-percentage looks as new Chargers coordinator Mike McDaniel.

Tagovailoa completed 66.2% of his passes in his first two seasons as a pro. By his second year with McDaniel, he was completing 69.3%; the next season, it was 72.9%. If Herbert elevates the offense beyond what Tagovailoa ever did -- a fair bet to make -- he might get a higher completion percentage as well.

Why find a new kid on the block? Burrow is the only quarterback save for Brees to produce multiple seasons over 70%, and he's entering 2026 with the best combo of offensive line and defensive play the Bengals have ever had in his tenure. Why does that matter? It should mean fewer snaps trailing in the fourth quarter in which he's forced to attempt high-difficulty throws ... and better protection when he has to take those obvious dropbacks. Even the Bengals' running game is in a healthy enough place to lead to fewer dropbacks overall.

This record feels so gettable because there are another six names I could put here. Goff fits with yet another season with Amon-Ra St. Brown, Jameson Williams and Sam LaPorta. Brock Purdy has two seasons at 69.4% and the most completion percentage-friendly playmaker in Christian McCaffrey. Dak Prescott, Mahomes, Allen and Maye are all candidates, too. Everyone is within range.

Fumbles forced
Current record holder: retired cornerback Charles "Peanut" Tillman (10 in 2012) and retired edge rusher Osi Umenyiora (10 in 2010)

Here's one I thought would benefit from the 17-game season but hasn't yet. In 2020, Ravens cornerback Marlon Humphrey forced eight fumbles, joining a thick tie for seventh all time. Just the year before, Steelers edge rusher T.J. Watt put up eight of his own. With an additional game joining the schedule in 2021, why wouldn't we get to nine?

It hasn't happened. In the past five seasons, only one player has reached seven (2021, Joey Bosa) and only four have produced six. The reason? Probably nothing in particular.

Pressure rate, sack rate and pressure-to-sack rate are all still better than historical rates. For whatever reason, fumble production just collapsed. In 2025, we saw the fewest forced fumbles on sacks (123) and forced fumbles on all plays (366) since 2000. Save for a huge rule change, a drop this big just feels like a blip. And if last year's fumble production was just a blip, then it doesn't mean we couldn't see a swing the other direction.

On an individual player level, we can also say with confidence that elite pass rushers are still getting to the quarterback consistently enough to potentially reach double-digit fumbles. With the right rusher in the right environment, the potential is still there.

It can be hard to find that right rusher. Umenyiora had seasons of four and five forced fumbles before his 10-strip-sack season appeared from nothingness. But we can narrow down the list by getting rid of power rushers, who don't excel in this field. We do know that speed rushers tend to be more productive than power rushers -- they're the ones who can swipe at the throwing arm as they run by a climbing quarterback.

During his sack-record-setting 2025 season, Myles Garrett had only three forced fumbles on his whopping 39 quarterback hits. Denver's Zach Allen somehow had zero on 47 QB hits, which might be a record in its own right. The powerful don't excel in this field.

So, could a speed rusher like Houston's Danielle Hunter get here? He had only three forced fumbles in 2025, but he benefits from a lack of attention opposite Will Anderson Jr. Can new Raven Trey Hendrickson reclaim his 2024 form, when he had six forced fumbles? Or what about Aidan Hutchinson (four forced fumbles in 2025) now playing with perhaps the best edge rotation behind him he has ever enjoyed in Detroit? Those are all established names of top-shelf rushers, but again, fumbles come with a lot of randomness. I wouldn't be surprised if Dallas Turner, Abdul Carter or Jalyx Hunt come knocking on this door.

There's a second avenue to a season with 11 forced fumbles: A back seven player. The Tillman route.

As completion percentage climbs along with scramble rate (see above), and as teams hand the ball off a little more, there are a ton of ball carriers available to strike. If fumbles at the quarterback really are declining, expect defensive coordinators to adjust and prioritize creating more loose balls in the secondary. Turnovers are king in the NFL; players and coaches alike will sell out to create them. Humphrey and San Francisco's Fred Warner are both excellent Peanut Punchers who could vie for the record. (*whispers* "Warner already has one and nearly had a second in Thursday's win over the Rams")

I'm buying low on the fumble market overall. Maybe it'll look bad when total fumbles forced comes in at another historic low this season. But if predicting broken records was easy, everyone would do it. You've got to get a little bold, and I'm resting my boldness on the balled fists of motivated defenders.

stories.headline: Indiana Pacers offseason recap, early 2026-27 season preview
stories.summary: Will Haliburton's return push the Pacers back to the top of the East? Looking back at the offseason and taking an early look at the 2026-27 season.
stories.body:
The Indiana Pacers have experienced some of the highest highs and lowest lows the NBA has to offer the last two season and they now enter the 2026-27 season healthy and with a fresh outlook.

Two-time All-Star Tyrese Haliburton returns after a torn Achilles in Game 7 of the 2025 Finals kept him out all of last season, and with him come the expectations that the Pacers will be back in the Eastern Conference playoff mix. Indiana missed out on a potential top four pick in June's draft, but still acquired Ivica Zubac at last year's trade deadline to pair with Haliburton.

Pascal Siakam also returns to help the Pacers bounce back from a 19-63 record last season, and the team brought in Kelly Oubre Jr. and Larry Nance Jr. to add depth to an already experienced roster.

Will Haliburton's return in Indianapolis be enough to make the Pacers a contender in the upgraded East?

ESPN's staff of experts is looking back at the offseason and taking an early look at the 2026-27 season for all 30 teams, with 30 pieces -- one for every team -- rolling out each weekday through Sept. 18. We're answering the biggest looming questions, evaluating X factors and much more for all 30 teams.

Quick links:

Roster | Depth chart | Transactions

More Pacers coverage | More NBA

Offseason at a glance
Key additions: Kelly Oubre Jr., Larry Nance Jr.

Key retentions: None

Key subtractions: C Micah Potter

The Pacers didn't make any major offseason changes, but they will have two major additions to the roster they were missing last year: starting center Ivica Zubac, who was acquired at the trade deadline from the Clippers, and star guard Tyrese Haliburton, returning from injury for the first time since the 2025 NBA Finals. Haliburton's presence lifted the Pacers into an Eastern Conference contender in 2024 and '25, and 16 months after a torn Achilles, they'll be counting on him to do the same in 2027. And Zubac will provide a different kind of center than Myles Turner provided the last time Haliburton was on the court. -- Jamal Collier

Zach Kram's offseason grade: B-

The Pacers embarked on their summer activity early, dealing a big package -- which included the eventual No. 5 pick -- for Ivica Zubac at the trade deadline in February.

Since the offseason began, they've focused exclusively on their bench, adding Kelly Oubre Jr. and Larry Nance Jr. on short-term deals. The next potential order of business is extension talks for Tyrese Haliburton and Pascal Siakam, though that's not a pressing concern because both players are still under contract for multiple years. -- Kram

What we learned over the past few months
From Ben Golliver's offseason lessons piece: Indiana has everything it needs for a bungee jump season.

The Pacers deservedly caught some grief over the finer points of their midseason trade for center Ivica Zubac, which wound up costing them the No. 5 pick in June's draft. Kevin Pritchard, Indiana's president, won't hear the end of it if Keaton Wagler blossoms into a star for the LA Clippers.

Nevertheless, Zubac is a clear upgrade over Myles Turner, Indiana's starting center during its surprising run to the 2025 Finals. After plummeting from 50 wins in 2024-25 to a 19-win gap season while franchise guard Tyrese Haliburton recovered from an Achilles injury, the Pacers are poised to bounce right back up the standings.

Finding a capable center was Indiana's top priority during Haliburton's absence, and Zubac outperformed Turner last season in scoring, rebounding, player efficiency rating and win shares. Otherwise, the Pacers bring back plenty of familiar faces from their Finals run, including Pascal Siakam, Aaron Nesmith, Andrew Nembhard, T.J. McConnell and Obi Toppin. Veteran coach Rick Carlisle hasn't gone anywhere, either.

Pessimists will argue that the Pacers caught lightning in a bottle two years ago, and that replicating their magical late-season run is too much to ask. Maybe so, but Haliburton's unique ability to get the most out of his teammates should restore Indiana to respectability. -- Golliver

The big question: How will the bench hold up?
Aside from Haliburton's brilliance and late game heroics, one the strengths for the Pacers during their NBA Finals run two seasons ago was the depth of their bench. Some of that depth has dwindled in the past year. Bennedict Mathurin has moved on, T.J. McConnell declined a bit last season without Haliburton and the Pacers haven't found another key reserve to pick up the slack. Rick Carlisle has been one of the best coaches in the league at pushing the right buttons with his rotation, and especially if the team plans to ease Haliburton back from injury at all, they will need to lean on their depth to get through the regular season. -- Collier

Basketball Power Index rank: No. 15
Here are the predicted Net Points per 100 possessions for the Pacers' top seven players for the 2026-27 season:

Haliburton was taken No. 12 in the 2020 draft and was quickly traded from his original team, but is arguably the best player from that Draft, ahead of No. 1 pick Anthony Edwards. He doesn't score as much and has been named only All-NBA Third Team compared to Edwards' Second Teams, but Haliburton has posted better performance across most player metrics: EPM, LEBRON, xRAPM, Net Points (not DARKO). -- Dean Oliver

Read about how Net Points works here.

Biggest injury returns for the 2026-27 NBA season

Biggest X factor
Ivica Zubac

Essentially the entire Pacers rotation that reached the 2024-25 Finals will return next season, with Haliburton back -- but with one key exception. Myles Turner fit into Indiana's system because of his shot-blocking prowess and 3-point spacing, but Zubac is a superior center overall. At his best, Zubac has been an All-Defensive honoree and All-NBA candidate.

He wasn't at his best last season, however, and now he's 29 years old, recovering from a broken rib and adjusting to a drastically different system than he's ever played in before. (He played just five games for the Haliburton-less Pacers after last season's trade.) Zubac might offer a lower floor than Turner, just because of his uncertain fit with the up-tempo Pacers. But his ceiling is much higher. -- Kram

Fantasy insight from our expert
Fantasy insight ahead of the season: The Pacers finished 12th in the NBA in assists last season (27.7 APG) with point guard Tyrese Haliburton sidelined, but they had finished third (29.2 APG) and first (30.8 APG) in the two seasons prior. With Haliburton back and running Coach Rick Carlisle's motion offense, the Pacers should again return to the top of the league in the category. And team assists lead to team points, which is good for the fantasy prospects of all Pacers rotation players.-- Andre Snellings

Odds by DraftKings Sportsbook at time of publication.
